prototype_questions.question: Which active-leader fence and Redis epoch-install protocol prevents a stale gate process from mutating state or issuing accepted permits across PostgreSQL lease loss and delayed Redis writes?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted service has separate PostgreSQL latch and Redis state stores. The local probe tested row-lock serialization and Redis stale-epoch rejection separately, but not delayed writes, lease loss, split brain, or permit issuance through one service protocol. Compare candidates with deterministic failure injection before selecting the implementation contract.
decision_criteria: stale leader cannot mutate Redis after a higher epoch is installed
no permit issuance when owner, lease, lock, or epoch is uncertain
bounded recovery when a delayed old-epoch command lands before installation
durable monotonic epoch behavior across REF-Q process restart; provider failover remains a separate PROD-Q qualification
bounded lock duration and simple operational recovery
lost PostgreSQL finalization and uncertain WAITAOF responses remain inhibited until reference-target evidence establishes the exact durable result
coordinated PostgreSQL and Redis restore cannot admit from mutually consistent stale snapshots on a supported wrapper path
each supported REF-Q restore path writes and fsyncs the host inhibit record before restoring either store; direct/provider restore, full-host rollback, and wrapper bypass are outside REF-Q guarantees
the current restore-episode ID invalidates pre-restore commands and permits on supported paths; unavailable or unverified control denies admission
resume release is idempotently bound to the audited RESUME command; admission remains denied until durable release acknowledgement

candidates.approach: Use a PostgreSQL owner/epoch row lock with server-time lease validation across each bounded Redis mutation or permit issue, install the leader epoch in Redis with a monotonic Lua compare-and-set, bind both stores to the externally verified restore-episode ID, and wait for the configured fsync threshold before serving.

Use a PostgreSQL transaction-scoped advisory lock plus a durable owner/epoch row compare-and-set, with the same monotonic Redis epoch installation and fsync barrier; deny work whenever either PostgreSQL signal is uncertain.

prototype_questions.question: How can command retries remain idempotent after one-year actor-audit deletion without retaining actor identity or operator reason indefinitely?
prototype_questions.rationale: PAUSE and RESUME command IDs must not produce duplicate transitions or become reusable with different requests. Actor/reason audit follows accepted retention policy A (minimum 365 days, then deletion within the qualified bounded window); command deduplication has a separate retention design. Prototype the smallest privacy-preserving option and measure storage/restore behavior.
decision_criteria: same command never advances generation twice
changed-request reuse is rejected after audit expiry

actor identity and operator reason are deleted on the accepted A deletion deadline of event time plus at most 365 days + 1 hour + 2 seconds, if epsilon <= 1 second and W <= 1 hour are qualified for every copy
minimal retained data and explainable backup/export deletion
recovery remains fail-closed after Redis or PostgreSQL restore
every authenticated duplicate retry is actor-attributed durably before returning the stored result
retrying the same command with a different audit-only reason returns the original state result, advances no generation, and records that retry separately
long-lived tombstones do not retain recoverable low-entropy operator reasons or require unsafe key retention
MAC rotation remains consistent across PostgreSQL, Redis, and every retained backup at every crash cut
NEW_ONLY cannot be declared while PostgreSQL/Redis tombstone key sets differ or any live tombstone lacks a valid new-key primary MAC
every actor/reason audit copy is securely deleted by its accepted A deadline (365 days plus at most 1 hour + 2 seconds under qualified bounds) without retaining it to preserve tombstones
the qualified timestamp error bound, tamper-evident inherited backup deadline, and restore/promotion rollback checks cannot shorten retention

candidates.approach: Keep a minimal PostgreSQL command tombstone indefinitely, separately from the one-year actor/reason audit, keyed by (restore_episode_id, command_id) and atomically mirrored by the Redis transition-result tombstone. Retain every non-sensitive canonical MAC input (API version, restore episode ID, action, expected latch epoch, expected current Redis generation, barrier generation, and opaque registration ID), keyed request MAC/key ID, and result status/code/generations. Exclude actor, reason, free-text, and personal identifiers. Use resumable cross-store re-MAC rotation with old/new MAC slots; prohibit key retirement until authoritative rows and retained backups have been migrated or expired.

Use a gate-minted immutable, signed request envelope whose opaque command ID binds the canonical request and expiry; deliver the envelope before execution and reject expired envelopes before any store lookup, then delete command-result rows after the maximum retry horizon while preserving one-year actor/reason audit.

prototype_questions.question: Which permit and identity-validation contract lets application instances reject forged, cross-instance, stale, and replayed permits while safely stopping new handlers within the accepted five-second limit during gate-service loss?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted design separates workload PAUSE from individual-operator RESUME and uses short-lived generation-bound permits. Issuer/audience validation, instance identity binding, signing-key rotation, and local handler-start validation must be testable without allowing a public ecommerce identity or caller-chosen instance ID to control the global gate.
decision_criteria: workload identity can PAUSE but cannot RESUME
only individually authenticated operators with the dedicated role can RESUME
permit binds verified subject to deployment, instance incarnation, leader, latch, and gate generations
permit binds an unpredictable signed request nonce to its outstanding issuance request
registration and drain proof bind a unique authenticated instance to a broker-observed connection, not caller-supplied identifiers
forged, stale, cross-instance, expired, and replayed permit responses reject; a currently installed valid lease may authorize multiple handler starts until expiry
lost gate connectivity stops new handler starts by the conservative five-second expiry
renewable lease issuance, lease replacement, and PAUSE have a tested linearization point; PAUSE blocks renewal and revoke stops new starts
per-instance lease renewal meets a predeclared replica-count and renewal-rate envelope with bounded latency and overload behavior
late lease responses cannot install a permit after PAUSE; nonce registration, network request, and local install/start increment have tested lock boundaries
permit temporal claims and fresh restore-episode binding are explicit; broker connection record IDs are provider-qualified as non-reusable or admission fails closed

candidates.approach: Use a gate-issued signed renewable short-lived lease with an epoch-scoped signing key and authenticated workload identity binding. A currently installed valid lease may authorize multiple handler starts until its conservative expiry, at most five seconds after the renewal request began. Enforce strict issuer/audience/algorithm/expiry checks and current leader-epoch bootstrap before admission.

Use an opaque permit reference bound to an authenticated instance registration and require an online gate-service admission check at each handler start; this stops earlier than the renewable-lease candidate during gate-service loss and must be evaluated against the accepted five-second availability behavior.

prototype_questions.question: How does the restore wrapper’s durable host inhibit reach every gate permit issuer and application instance, remaining fail-closed across gate restart, lost notification, and partial restore?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted REF-Q design puts the restore episode in a root-owned host control record outside the service backup domains, while the gate service issues admission permits. The wrapper must confirm that every issuer observes the current episode before any restore starts, and stale/unavailable observations must deny admission. The observation/acknowledgement path is not selected and can change the reference design.
decision_criteria: wrapper durably records INHIBITED before any supported restore and cannot report success until every active permit issuer confirms the exact episode and generation, or all issuer processes are proven stopped with automatic restart fenced for the restore window
gate restart, lost or delayed notification, partial restore, and stale host-record read never permit admission

permit issuance/install/start is serialized against observation of INHIBITED; an issuer stops new permit responses and acknowledges the exact episode only after pending responses are fenced or reconciled
application drain, readiness-down, and channel closure account for already-issued permits, prefetched deliveries, and active handlers before any service-store restore begins
a stale but well-formed ACTIVE host record is rejected against an independently trusted fresh expected episode/generation; the freshness source and its trust boundary are explicit

all registered app instances stop new handler starts and readiness remains down until audited RESUME for the exact episode; RESUME rejects stale registrations unless each instance has a current-episode drain acknowledgement or the exact broker connection has an accepted fencing/closure proof

no root write capability is granted to the gate service; exact host path ownership/mode, mount identity, gate UID/GID/capabilities, read-only enforcement, path-substitution defense, and record integrity are verified
crash cuts around host-record fsync/rename, gate observation, drain, store restore, audited RESUME, and host-inhibit release reconcile idempotently

if the selected mechanism reads the host record on the admission path, synchronous read latency, failures, and resource cost are measured separately on the accepted reference capacity sweep; process-quiescence alternatives measure shutdown, restart-fence, and recovery costs
host loss, root compromise, full-host rollback, and wrapper bypass remain explicitly outside REF-Q guarantees

candidates.approach: Candidate only; the local mount probe favors a read-only directory mount over an individual-file mount on the observed Docker Desktop host. The wrapper writes a complete temporary record, fsyncs it, atomically renames it over the current record, and fsyncs the directory. Before selection, define and test an independently fresh expected episode/generation, serialize each gate's permit issue/install path against PAUSE observation, fence pending responses before exact-episode acknowledgement, prove deployment least privilege/path integrity, and measure synchronous record-read cost. Unavailable, malformed, stale, or unreadable state denies admission.

Use an authenticated wrapper-to-gate inhibit/release API with durable episode and acknowledgement state; gate restart bootstraps from the host record before it may issue permits, and the wrapper waits for every issuer acknowledgement. A gate that has not observed the current episode must deny permits; an API-only notification path is insufficient after a lost request unless an additional fresh host-control signal prevents stale ACTIVE admission.

Candidate only; after durably recording the new INHIBITED episode, the wrapper blocks external admission, drains app instances and closes Rabbit consumer channels, then stops every app and gate issuer process. Before restoring any store it verifies all registered instances and issuer processes are stopped, broker connections are closed, and the local supervisor/restart policy cannot start stale processes during the restore window. It restarts the gate through a protected wrapper-controlled path bound to the exact host-record episode in sticky INHIBITED mode, reconciles restored stores, obtains audited RESUME, releases the host inhibit, then starts apps. RESUME must reject stale registrations unless each has a current-episode drain acknowledgement or the exact broker connection has an accepted fencing/closure proof; stopping a container alone is not that proof. Missing/stale startup binding or any uncertain process/connection inventory denies restore or admission. This avoids per-permit mount polling but shifts the proof burden to process-manager fencing, startup binding, and crash recovery; wrapper bypass, root compromise, and full-host rollback remain excluded.
